articles.title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
articles.content: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code. We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement. Our rationale is outlined below. The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools ( comparator and con-leche –compare ), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/ . These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources. Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification. We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.
articles.summary: Lean 与 Mathlib 社区宣布 Levent Alpöge 以 1700 万行 Lean 代码形式发布黎曼猜想证明，引发形式化验证界关注。

articles.title: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
articles.content: Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite! My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed. I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency. But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR . I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦 The setup # MacBook Pro M3 Pro 2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my WiFi 7 debugging post What I thought was interesting # Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know. I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again. So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason. The driver and flow control # The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website , so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault. Then I tried flow control . I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when

articles.title: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
articles.content: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs Raph Levien, November 21, 2026 This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs , published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey ), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI. Rust GUI is still compelling The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative. Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia. The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance? For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things. Native is complicated My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria. I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent

articles.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'
articles.content: A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades. In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission. Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally. Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans. A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread. He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said. “The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.” Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth. There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations. Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers. “These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the w
articles.summary: 药物 daraxonrasib 在试验中使十二分之一患者胰腺肿瘤消失，被称为数十年来该癌症最大突破。

articles.title: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory
articles.content: LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler. It measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the output when compressed. It then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage. On Gemma 4 E2B, its GGUF has 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size. The method and every result are on the site . The code is under the MIT license. LookAtMyQuant 2: Qwen3.5-4B in 1.2 GB LookAtMyQuant 2 takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB, 2.3 bits per weight. The file solves 330 of 540 exact-answer math problems. Prism ML's Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B solves 328 at 1.20 GB, and the original solves 359. Its KL from the original on held-out text is 0.45 nats, against 0.59 for Bonsai. The recipe is post-training quantization with trellis codes, calibrated on the model's own worked math solutions with digit tokens weighted 10×, and with bits allocated per row by Fisher information. 4,000 steps of distillation follow, in which every layer is re-quantized once from the original weights. The page has the findings, the full recipe and its cost, about $34 of GPU time. The recipe's code is here, and the next section runs it. The 1.23 GB file itself is the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release , packed for the Apple Silicon runtime. The same recipe takes Qwen3.8-27B from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB, 2.1 bits per weight, calibrated and distilled on English prose and chat, code and math. The file solves 401 of the 540 math problems, as many as the original, and Unsloth's UD-IQ2_XXS GGUF of the same size solves 348. It also scores above that GGUF on HumanEval (73.8% against 67.1%), MMLU (78.8% against 75.0%) and GSM8K (94.5% against 92.7%). Beside it sits a 4-bit DSpine drafter (1.02 GB, converted from tencent/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16 with runtime_mlx/convert_dspine.py and packed with pack_drafter.py ), which roughly doubles decode speed on math and code on Apple silicon. Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB, 8.9 GB, 11.2 GB, and 12.8 GB Extended to a 26.4B physical / 5.4B active 3×-looped MoE ( L6–17 looped 3× = 48 logical visits, 128 experts top-8), the compiler and full-MoE proximal fine-tuning ( SQYFR ) compress thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini from 18.89 GB of text weights into four Apple Silicon MLX builds: 5.38 GB ( 1.65 bpp ) , 8.87 GB ( 2.72 bpp ) , 11.18 GB ( 3.43 bpp ) , and 12.76 GB ( 3.92 bpp ) — combining 4 KB SRAM hashed block-vector trellis codes ( ht2 / ht3 ), row trellis codes ( rtr1 / rtr4 ), a tr2 floor on the tail lm_head bucket ( head.7 ), and exact native NVFP4 passthrough ( 69/192 and 109/192 highest-sensitivity expert buckets kept at 0.0 error in the 11.2 GB and 12.8 GB builds). Evaluated untruncated ( max_new_tokens = 1,536 , greedy, reasoning_effort="none" ) on the same BF16 teacher, openai/gsm8k ( test[:200] ), all 164 executable openai/openai_humaneval problems, 4 Vision VQA tests (with the untouched 637 MB BF16 vision tower), and 16+13-language TextMix windows: Model Text GB Text bpp free_KL ( en/chat/code ) all13_KL GSM8K (200) HumanEval (164) Vision
articles.summary: LookAtMyQuant 量化编译器让 Gemma 4 E2B 模型以 5.4GB 内存运行，同体积下 KL 散度比 Q4_K_M 低 12 倍。

articles.title: PostgreSQL Extensions in Go
articles.content: PostgreSQL extensions in Go gopgext builds PostgreSQL extensions from plain Go code, using TinyGo. Mark a function with //gopgext:function and it becomes a SQL function: gopgext writes the C glue, the install script and the control file. Get started Documentation GitHub Experimental gopgext is experimental. Don’t use it in production: a bug in the generated code or the Go runtime runs inside the server, where it can crash it or corrupt data, and the API and generated SQL may change without notice. Just Go A project is plain Go files. The standard library works: fmt , regexp , encoding/json , crypto/* , maps, generics, iterators, defer / recover . Types map to SQL Strings, numbers, arrays, NULL s, sets, rows, timestamps, UUIDs and JSON map to SQL types. Define your own data types and composite types in Go. Queries and errors Run SQL through SPI, return errors with SQLSTATE codes, log, read settings and stay responsive to query cancellation. Beyond functions Write triggers, aggregates, GiST, GIN, SP-GiST and BRIN operator classes, index access methods, foreign data wrappers and query hooks. Proven on contrib Ports of PostgreSQL’s contrib modules ( pgcrypto , hstore , pg_stat_statements , cube , …) pass upstream’s regression tests. Safe coexistence Several Go extensions load in one backend. PostgreSQL errors never unwind through Go frames, and results are copied into PostgreSQL memory. Hello, world # package main import ( "strings" "gopgext/pg" ) // Hello returns a greeting for name. // //gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe func Hello ( name string ) string { return "Hello, " + name + "!" } // Shout upper-cases s. An empty string raises an error. // //gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe func Shout ( s string ) ( string , error ) { if s == "" { return "" , pg . Errorf ( pg . CodeInvalidParameterValue , "nothing to shout" ) } return strings . ToUpper ( s ) + "!" , nil } func main () {} // runs once per backend, when PostgreSQL loads the library gopgext init hello # creates hello/go.mod and hello/main.go gopgext install hello # builds hello.so, hello.control, hello--1.0.sql and installs them psql -c 'CREATE EXTENSION hello' -c "SELECT hello('world')" # hello # --------------- # Hello, world! The tutorial walks through it step by step. A sibling project # gopgext uses the same approach as gokm , which builds Linux kernel modules from Go: a custom TinyGo target and runtime layer for the host, a C runtime compiled by the host’s own build system (PGXS here, kbuild there), and generated glue.
articles.summary: gopgext 借助 TinyGo 让开发者用纯 Go 编写 PostgreSQL 扩展，自动生成 C 胶水代码与安装脚本，目前为实验性项目。

articles.title: Show HN: Zero C# – C# without a runtime or GC
articles.content: C# with nothing underneath A fork of bflat compiles C# straight to a small native program: no .NET runtime, no garbage collector, nothing to install where it runs. You keep C#'s syntax, type checking and generics. Memory comes from arenas you free all at once, and a small library gives you strings, collections, input and output on those terms. The same source runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, on WebAssembly, and on DOS on a 386. Get started Build the quiz tutorial Run it in your browser // Read into a stack buffer: nothing allocated per answer. Span < char > buffer = stackalloc char [ 32 ]; Out .Write( $"Q {i} : {a} + {b} = " ); int length = In .ReadLine(buffer); // Kept until the end, so it goes into an arena. mistakes.Add( Str .Format(keep, $" {a} + {b} = {a + b} , not {value} " )); From the quiz the tutorial builds, step by step. The language stays, the runtime goes The compiler still checks everything it checks in .NET. What's missing is what a runtime would do while your program runs. You keep C# 15 Unions, extension members and the new memory safety rules. Real generics A specialized copy for each type, and static abstract members. Interfaces and virtual methods Default interface methods, casts, is and as . Records, tuples, anonymous types Value equality, with , and the generated ToString . Lambdas and queries Where , Select and GroupBy , from a small library instead of LINQ. Threads Parallel.For runs a loop on every core. You do without Garbage collector Arenas free their memory all at once, when you say. .NET runtime Hello world is 11 KB on Windows and 40 KB on Linux, with nothing to install. Catching exceptions throw ends the program. Return errors as unions. Reflection and async A type can be compared, but it has no name. One program, five machines The hello-world sample, unchanged, built for each target. Each build is checked by the same test suite, which requires the same output everywhere. $ ./build.sh Minimal $ ./run.sh Minimal Hello from zero-mode! $ wc -c bin/Minimal 39848 bin/Minimal Linux, x64 or arm64 A native program that needs only the C library. On macOS it builds and runs in a container. $ ./build.sh --mac Minimal $ bin/mac/Minimal Hello from zero-mode! $ wc -c bin/mac/Minimal 64728 bin/mac/Minimal macOS on Apple Silicon A native Mac program: bflat compiles it, the Mac's own clang links it. No container to run it. $ ./build.sh --win Minimal $ ./run.sh --win Minimal Hello from zero-mode! $ wc -c bin/win/Minimal.exe 10752 bin/win/Minimal.exe Windows x64 A console program on Windows' own C library, built from Linux or macOS. Tested under Wine. $ ./build.sh --wasm Minimal $ ./run.sh --wasm Minimal Hello from zero-mode! $ wc -c bin/wasm/Minimal.wasm 15833 bin/wasm/Minimal.wasm WebAssembly A WASI module, through NativeAOT-LLVM. Runs under wasmtime. C:\>D: D:\>PROGRAM Hello from zero-mode! D:\>DIR PROGRAM.EXE PROGRAM EXE 16,384 D:\> DOS on a 386 The same bitcode compiled for a 386, run by the HX DOS extender. Tested on Bochs's i38
articles.summary: bflat 分支 Zero C# 可将 C# 直接编译为原生程序，无需 .NET 运行时和 GC，保留语法、类型检查与泛型。

articles.title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
articles.content: Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone. But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine. This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox. As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU. Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test. Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed. One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step. That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen. The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door. Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.
articles.summary: 文章分析欧盟 DMA 生效后 iOS 浏览器选择增加、Firefox 日活翻倍，但 WebKit 仍垄断 iOS 内核的原因。

articles.title: TODOs JJ Style
articles.content: _______________________ < todo: fill out cowsay > ----------------------- \ ^__^ \ (oo)\_______ (__)\ )\/\ ||----w | || || I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me. In-Tree TODO is Kinda Annoying Usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard. But, I forget about this file quickly and am not very good at remembering to cross stuff off. Also since it’s in-tree I’ll often not want to update it, and then forget to do so later. Empty Commits to the Rescue JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work. So what if I just make all the stuff I wanna do later as empty commits? Pretty nice! When I want to start working on something I’ll rebase it out of my TODO tree and onto some other change. I need to rebase my “TODO base” forward when i make changes, but because it’s empty it will never have conflicts and can pretty easily move around. TODOs that depend on other TODOs also naturally fit here, I just make new empty commits on top of other empty commits. Keeping Them Private I have git.private-commits configured to make sure nothing with the private: prefix will get pushed. This ensures my TODOs stay on my local system. Of course, there are benefits to not doing this. # In Home Manager... programs . jujutsu . settings . git . private-commits = "description('private:*')" ; Anyway that’s about it, not very ground breaking but something I like.
articles.summary: 作者分享使用 Jujutsu（jj）版本控制时管理 TODO 的新方法，替代传统 TODO.md 文件的工作流。

articles.content: [2026-11-20] I'm proud to announce the second release of Vim Classic, Vim Classic 8.3.1, a stable, long-term support fork of the ubiquitous text editor, maintained without the assistance of generative AI tools. For more information about the motivations for this fork, please read this blog post . This release includes applicable Vim patches up to Vim 8.2.3237, including numerous bug fixes, minor features, and compatibility improvements for Vim plugins. This release also removes Python 2 support from Vim Classic. Vim Classic is charityware, much like Vim, and we are happy to continue supporting Bram's passion of providing for children in need in Uganda. Switching from Vim to Vim Classic would be an opportune moment for you to make a donation ! You can download Vim Classic from SourceHut: .tar.gz vim-classic-v8.3.1.tar.gz .tar.gz.sig vim-classic-v8.3.1.tar.gz.sig This release is signed with my PGP public key . Please subscribe to vim-classic-announce to be notified of important (actionable) news and releases in the future. Last, but not least, let me extend a big "thanks!" to everyone who jumped in to enthusiastically test Vim Classic, provide feedback, and contribute many patches and backports to get this release done. Happy editing! — Drew DeVault

articles.title: Announcing jj-musubi: live sync for Jujutsu
articles.content: I’m pleased to announce a new source control tool, jj-musubi , that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu ( jj ) repository across multiple machines. Every time jj snapshots my work, jj-musubi syncs it to every machine in moments, and also commits, rebases, fetches, and so on. This simple capability is surprisingly powerful. I often work on one machine, and build or test on others. Now they get my changes as I make them, and I don’t need to remember whether I was editing on my laptop or someplace else. If I fetch changes from or push changes to upstream, all of my copies stay up to date. jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git). It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model). Things you can do Jujutsu already treats the working copy as a commit. Running jj status records a snapshot of my edits in that commit, which jj-musubi then syncs to my other machines. I like to have my shell prompt run jj status , so in practice I rarely have to think about snapshots. jj-musubi does not write to the working copy. Each machine has its own working copy and workspaces as usual, so syncs of commits, snapshots, and rewrites can bring in new history while a build is running, without changing the files under it. On a laptop, I can work offline, and my machine will sync when I’m back on the network. This has also proven handy when I have agents working on several machines. I can give each agent its own jj workspace on different systems, then run jj diff -r devbox/agent-1@ on the laptop to see what one of them has done so far. If one finds a bug that another needs to fix, they can coordinate and see each other’s work without overhead. Ephemeral uses jj-musubi refers to a collection of copies of a repo as a hive . I often run agents in temporary disposable VMs. jj-musubi supports this by allowing an agent to lease its repo’s membership in the hive: if it doesn’t renew that lease in time, its repo gets forgotten about, so temporary repos or vanished containers can’t just stack up and clutter things. Why I wanted this Back when I was at Meta, I kicked off the project that became Sapling and Mononoke. Sapling’s Commit Cloud gives engineers there a similar way to move work between machines, and Google engineers have something similar with an internal jj server. articles.title: Probabilistic data structures in Go, part 2
articles.content: Probabilistic data structures in Go, part 2 Probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle. Does the set contain a certain item? How many unique items are in the collection? What is the 99th percentile in a stream of numbers? How similar are two sets? Unlike deterministic structures, the answers might not be exact, but in return, you can save a lot of memory. Previously, we reviewed the following data structures : Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items). In this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered. We'll look at how they work and what kinds of guarantees they provide. All examples use unsure — a package that implements these structures in Go. Binary fuse filter • UltraLogLog • Log-linear histogram • MinHash Binary fuse filter A binary fuse filter is a set that trades certainty for space, like a Bloom filter . It can tell you that an item is definitely not in the set, or that it probably is (which might be a false positive). The filter doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set. Unlike a Bloom filter, a binary fuse filter is static: you build it once from all the items, and you can't add more later. In exchange, it uses less memory than a Bloom filter with the same false positive rate. For example, a fuse filter for 1,000,000 items with a 0.39% false positive rate takes 1.13 MB (9 bits per item), while a Bloom filter takes 1.51 MB (12 bits per item). This makes binary fuse filters a good fit for data that is written once and read many times, like the key set of an immutable file in a database (to skip files that don't have the key), or a list of known bad items, such as leaked passwords or malicious URLs. items := [][] byte {[] byte ( "alice" ), [] byte ( "bob" )} // An 8-bit filter: 0.39% false positive rate. filter := fuse . New [ uint8 ]( slices . Values ( items ), len ( items )) filter . Contains ([] byte ( "alice" )) // true filter . Contains ([] byte ( "carol" )) // false (or, rarely, true) The fingerprint type ( T in New[T] ) determines the false positive rate and the memory use: Type False positive rate Bits per item uint8 0.39% 9 uint16 0.0015% 18 uint32 2.3e-10 36 The constructor takes an iterator of items to add to the filter and the expected number of items (0 if unknown). The number is only used to preallocate memory, so a good estimate makes the build faster. You can check if an item is in the filter, but you cannot add or delete an item, count the number of items, or iterate over them. How it works The filter is an array of b -bit fingerprints (for example, b = 8 for uint8 ). Each item is hashed to a 64-bit value h , which gives the item's fingerprint f (b bits computed from h) and three positions in the array (cells

articles.title: C++26 is done (again)! — Trip report: November 2026 ISO C++ standards meeting (Búzios, Brazil)
articles.content: tl;dr: A few highlights C++26 technical work, originally completed in March, was reopened and is now recompleted: The anticipated plan is to reissue the updated C++26 document for a second approval ballot. Most of the six-day meeting was devoted to addressing a second set of international comments for C++26, primarily on the contracts language feature. Adopted this week for draft C++29: break label; continue label; , std::ranges::any_view , views::slice , and more… Overview Today, the ISO C++ committee completed technical work on C++26 for a second time in beautiful Búzios, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (hybrid online via Zoom). As I reported in March , the ISO C++ committee completed technical work on C++26 at our March meeting; following that, we held the first meeting of C++29 in June . Since then, the approval (Draft International Standard, or DIS) ballot for C++26 was held but, for the first time, did not pass unanimously and was sent back to the ISO C++ committee with additional international comments to address, mostly about the contracts feature ( pre , post , and contract_assert ). So this week we addressed the additional comments on C++26, including by adopting an extension to contracts and providing a detailed rationale and timeline to inform national bodies of the history and process by which contracts were developed, concerns heard repeatedly, and decisions made. The committee is now producing an updated final document that is anticipated to be sent out for its second international approval (DIS) ballot and final editorial work, anticipated to be published in the near future by ISO. This meeting was hosted by C++ Alliance . Thank you to everyone involved and especially to Matheus Izvekov , who took the lead in making the arrangements! Our hosts arranged for high-quality facilities for our six-day meeting from Monday through Saturday. We had about 220 attendees, split about 35%/65% in-person/remote-Zoom, formally representing 27 nations. (The higher-than-usual percentage of remote participation was partly because of the U.S. aviation ground stop that disrupted air travel just as experts were trying to fly to the ISO C++ meeting.) At each meeting we have new guest attendees, and this time there were 13 new guests, mostly in person, in addition to new attendees who are official national body representatives. To all of them, once again welcome! The committee currently has 22 active subgroups, but this time fewer of them met throughout the week than usual as we focused on the additional C++26 comments. C++26, take 2 The most controversial feature in C++26 is contracts: pre , post , and contract_assert . The committee already had strong consensus, and as of the end of this meeting has still stronger consensus, on including the feature in C++26, but we spent most of this meeting rehearing contracts concerns and working hard again to address them. articles.title: How I Got Postgres into a Single Binary
articles.content: SQLite, but Postgres SQLite is one of my favorite database technologies. It's a full SQL database, designed as an embeddable library, that stores all its data in a single file. The sqlite3 command line tool is great too. You point it at a file and run queries. There's no server to run. At the other end of the spectrum is Postgres. It's the most capable general purpose SQL database, trusted in production at scale, and is something of an industry standard. With that comes complexity, starting with the fact that it's client-server. SQLite is a natural fit for software that needs a database but isn't meant to be deployed in the cloud at scale: desktop apps, self-hosted tools, things you run locally. These applications can use SQLite and manage it themselves, so you barely know there's a database involved. So when you find self-hostable open source software you'd like to run on your own computer, it can be daunting when it says it requires Postgres. Now you're responsible for setting up a database and getting it ready for the software to use. Sure, you can run Postgres in Docker, and plenty of projects recommend it. But now you have two dependencies. If you don't already have Docker, you have to install it, which can mean a VM and a daemon on your machine. Then you have to run Postgres in it and make sure it's running whenever you use the software. That's a lot just to try something you don't know you want yet. Wouldn't it be great to have the SQLite experience, but with Postgres? That's miniPG . It isn't Postgres as a library. There's already a WASM project for that, reasonably called PGlite . miniPG is closer to the SQLite CLI: a single program that embeds a full Postgres server and client, wrapped up so you can use it the way you'd use sqlite3 . Point it at a path, that path becomes the database, and you can run queries against it right away. There's no server to set up or keep running. Jumping into a new Postgres database to try something out or debug it is now easier than using Postgres in a Docker container, and you don't need Docker at all. And miniPG still provides a fully functional Postgres server for software that needs one. In many cases, you can just launch an open source program that looks for its Postgres config in the environment with miniPG. miniPG in 30 seconds miniPG comes as a single, self-contained executable. You can just point it at a directory and run a query. There's no server to start, nothing to configure, and the result comes back immediately. minipg ./mydb "create table notes (id serial, body text)" minipg ./mydb "insert into notes (body) values ('hello')" minipg ./mydb "select * from notes" That directory is the database. When nothing is using it, it's just files on disk. You can copy it, back it up, or delete it. This is actually real Postgres, not a compatibility layer, and this binary compiles to Mac, Windows, and Linux. When some software expects a Postgres server, miniPG can be one: minipg serve ./mydb -p 5432 Like I

from mojang. to my surprise, they weren’t asking me to shut my project down, but rather asking if i could help them debug an issue with my api. attached was a screenshot of their “investigation tool”. their tool showed that mojang was also using other services like mcscans and the one from cornbread2100 . at this point i still had no clue what they were using the data for, but i didn’t really care, because i had mojang, the company behind minecraft, as one of my users, which to me was really cool. so of course i helped them fix their issue. banned servers though my views on mojang did eventually change. one day i stumbled upon this reddit post where op talked about getting an email from mojang, forwarded by their isp, saying their minecraft server violated mojang’s guidelines. now this articles.title: Changes on freedesktop.org
articles.content: Today we launched a change that has been a long time in the making: The updated website for freedesktop.org , as well as the refreshed wiki.freedesktop.org are live now! You can read the announcement here , this blog post elaborates a bit on it and on the background of the changes, as well as future plans. Why change anything? The freedesktop.org website has been a wiki for a long time, which definitely was the right call in its inception. A wiki is very much in spirit of Freedesktop’s mission statement to foster collaboration between desktop environments and to be a place to create de-facto standards. However, over the years, working with the wiki became a bit of an issue: Not only did we face multiple spam-apocalypses (which in part motivated the switch to IkiWiki in 2013 and resulted in us heavily restricting write access to the wiki), but it also meant that official project information, finished specifications, half-finished proposals and pages nobody had touched in fifteen years were all sitting next to each other. Since 2000 when Freedesktop.org was started, the project has grown so much and has had so many associated projects and specifications over the decades that it is now very difficult for new people to get an overview what is current and what state the software projects and specifications hosted by Freedesktop.org are in. Having only a wiki as a large and somewhat disorganized pile of information did not help with that issue, so I worked to split things up: We now have a website as well as a wiki, using different designs to distinguish the two, and serving different purposes. Website & website plans The website at www.freedesktop.org will be the place for “official”, or rather, more curated information. Now that the new website is live, its content is still largely that of the old wiki. Over the next weeks, I will be working on cleaning up its contents and listings. For example, I will clearly split active projects from archived ones, add missing ones, and also work towards synchronizing the specifications hosted on the former wiki / website with the ones listed on specifications.fd.o . So, basically I will do an inventory check of Freedesktop. That work has already started, but until now, I could not make any public changes to not disrupt workflows or make my own future work harder by having diverging information in two places (website & wiki). I also wanted to make it easier for people to find information on how to get involved with Freedesktop and associated projects, so the new website now has a more discoverable section for that. The new website is a static site hosted via GitLab Pages and using Pelican . You can view its sources if you like. Wiki changes Of course, we also still want to keep the Wiki and all of its rich history around! It remains the easy-to-edit place for collaboration on upcoming projects and specifications. articles.content: Google recently detailed how three interacting bugs across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, and the Linux kernel caused intermittent Kubernetes API connectivity failures, blocking around 800 developers from deploying to production. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: 谷歌披露GKE API超时源于GKE、Private Service Connect与Linux内核三个交互缺陷，曾致约800名开发者无法部署。

articles.title: Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities
articles.content: Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Meta推出TLX，作为Triton低层扩展，弥合高层GPU编程抽象与底层硬件控制之间的差距。

articles.title: Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS
articles.content: Uber redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while maintaining a cache hit rate above 99.9% and p99 disk-backed cache miss latency below 100 microseconds. The hybrid architecture combines in-memory keys and frequently accessed values with disk-backed storage, reducing garbage-collection overhead and memory consumption. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Uber重构Go翻译缓存，初始内存降低超90%，命中率保持99.9%以上，p99未命中延迟低于100微秒。

articles.title: Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale
articles.content: Google has announced it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: 谷歌将Agent Substrate和gVisor捐赠给CNCF，把AI代理基础设施置于厂商中立的开源治理之下。

articles.title: Presentation: Modernising Retail at Scale: Architecting a Cloud‑to‑Edge Platform for a Global Enterprise
articles.content: Jayesh Bhayani discusses Tesco’s decade-long enterprise transformation from fragmented legacy systems to a unified cloud-edge platform. He explains how aligning system, talent, and process modernizations allowed Tesco to scale mission-critical retail operations to millions of customers, while sharing practical lessons on build vs. buy, cloud cost management, and preparing for agentic commerce. By Jayesh Bhayani
articles.summary: Tesco工程师分享十年转型：从碎片化遗留系统到统一云边平台，支撑数百万用户的零售关键业务。

articles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: The Future of Apache Iceberg
articles.content: Apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside new capabilities for data management and schema evolution. Daniel Weeks, co-creator of Apache Iceberg and member of technical staff at Databricks, presented a session at QCon San Francisco on the fourth version of the Apache Iceberg open table format specification. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: Apache Iceberg联合创始人Daniel Weeks在QCon旧金山介绍V4版本，重新设计表元数据以提升可扩展性并支持更频繁写入。

articles.title: Article: Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover
articles.content: Cloud SLAs promise uptime statistically, not absolutely. This article shows how to treat observability as a control plane that detects regional degradation, triggers automated failover, and confirms recovery rather than paging a human. Covers active-active architecture, DNS TTL pitfalls, composite Prometheus alerting, Route 53 weighted routing, and confirmation loops backed by a real S3 outage. By Saurabh Ahuja
articles.summary: InfoQ文章提出将可观测性作为多云容灾控制平面，自动检测区域故障并触发切换，减少人工介入。

articles.title: AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents
articles.content: AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free, CC0-licensed local stand-in for more than 200 of its services, generated from its public API models and aimed at the test loops of coding agents. AWS says agents wrote and maintain all of the code and publishes per-release fidelity scores. The docs say it does not evaluate IAM, and practitioners are split on trusting an emulator nobody reviewed. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: AWS发布免费本地模拟器，覆盖200多项服务，代码全部由AI代理编写维护，用于加速编码代理测试。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #544: AI is now the most-cited risk in the Fed's survey: 87%, up from 50%
articles.content: The Federal Reserve asked its market contacts what could shake the financial system, and 87% named AI, up from 50% in the spring. The same week, the FAA halted flights nationwide days after putting an AI tool in every regional control center, and says it is still looking at what happened. Nvidia's board has approached Arm's CEO about replacing Jensen Huang. Russian pranksters got three OpenAI national security staff on a video call. In the middle: Anthropic prices its IPO on Wednesday with $900.9 billion in compute commitments on its books.
articles.summary: 美联储调查显示87%受访者将AI列为金融系统最大风险，较春季的50%大幅上升，同期FAA因AI工具暂停全国航班。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #543: Google is the latest tech giant to chase TypeSafe's 8-week-old Jev
articles.content: This issue is about decision models, a new kind of AI model that does not write text. You give it an input and a fixed list of answers, and it returns the best answer with a probability, in milliseconds. TypeSafe AI released the first one, Jev, on September 15. On Wednesday Google released its own, after OpenAI and Microsoft did in October, and all three charge $0.10 or less per million input tokens and nothing for output. Shanghai AI Lab says its 4B model beat Jev on its tests, and Microsoft built its model on Alibaba's Qwen. Chatbots still score a little higher on the hardest decisions, at 15 times the cost. In the middle: on Vercel's gateway, decision models took one in four AI requests in October.
articles.summary: TypeSafe推出不生成文本的决策模型Jev，输入问题即返回带概率的最佳答案，谷歌随后发布同类模型跟进。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: AI周报前瞻：美国36场州长选举中最多15场或由支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人胜出，苹果、AMD将发布财报。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: 微软、Alphabet、亚马逊将陆续发布财报，市场关注AI投入回报，CoreWeave债务违约保险成本已升至困境水平。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，部分公司大量工作由AI代理完成，测试代理持续扩张。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 中期选举中AI生成或增强的广告支出超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI，最大亲AI超级政治行动委员会向空壳公司支付约2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能家电等家庭设备，引发安全担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶尖AI模型在自主开展AI研究的测试中失败，业界关注AI能否独立做研究及治理话语权归属。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，同时大规模部署进入日常使用，AI被限制或撤出的场景也在增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝Turnitin AI训练条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: A seminal moment in computing
articles.content: MG, founder and CEO of WorkOS, is back to talk about leading a company through what DHH called a seminal moment in computing. He explains Atlas, the AI coworker WorkOS built for itself and then launched, why agents will soon choose and sign up for your tech stack, and why this moment feels closer to fire than to the iPhone. Then he gets practical: starting a company is easier than ever, but product-market fit is harder, so be a heat-seeking missile for pain, pick customers you like, and stop calling yourself non-technical.
articles.summary: WorkOS CEO谈AI同事Atlas，认为智能体将自主选择并注册技术栈，称正处计算史关键节点。

articles.title: Orbin' with Amp
articles.content: Quinn Slack is back and we're talking about the next level for Amp. Agents write the code, they review the code, and they can push it to main (like our friends at Amp). But where should your agents live? Who remembers what you actually asked them to do? Amp is now its own company, and Quinn has a lot to say about orbs, threads that last forever, and why code review as we know it is fading. He explains why the model matters less than it used to, and why he worries we could lose the open source commons. Quinn even built a feature request live on the show to solve my tailnet problem.
articles.summary: Amp独立成公司，Quinn Slack谈智能体写代码、审代码并推送主干的下一阶段发展。

articles.title: All your packages are belong to us
articles.content: AI agents can write the code, choose the packages, and run the install. Who's checking what they just invited onto your machine? This week I'm joined by Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm. We get into the trust built into a package install, the new ways attackers are using agents, and what it takes to keep building without handing over the keys or your wallet.
articles.summary: Socket CTO谈AI智能体自动选包安装带来的供应链安全风险，以及攻击者利用智能体的新手法。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr提出'Kerr定律'，指出团队最大瓶颈是成员心智模型与实际构建成果脱节。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens谈Postgres扩展生态，pg_lake引入DuckDB与Iceberg，并分析AI对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha谈用Go重写支撑300万用户的邮件服务，并布局面向智能体的产品。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw作者谈40小时周末项目如何成为爆款开源并发展为AI企业，主打容器隔离安全。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out. I’ll be joined by three builders pushing this idea forward, starting with Dan Robinson from Detail (detail.dev), with more guests to be announced very soon. I also have 80 limited edition t-shirts printed to give away! This won’t be a few presentations followed by everyone heading home. We’re doing this Changelog-style: live conversations, questions from the room, drinks, and plenty of time afterward for the hallway track. If you’re in San Francisco, register to come hang out! Changelog IRL Thursday, September 17th, 2026 6:00pm – 9:00pm PDT PlanetScale HQ 108 Natoma St, San Francisco, CA 94105 Speakers Dan Robinson, (Detail) Christian Glassiognon, Developer Educator at PlanetScale TBD Schedule 6:00 - 6:45pm: Doors open, food, drinks and networking 6:45 - 7:00pm: Welcome and opening chat with Adam 7:00 - 8:00pm: Changelog IRL with Dan and special guests 8:00 - 8:15pm: Questions 8:30 - 9:00pm: Hanging out and networking 9:00pm: Close All times Pacific. PlanetScale HQ, 108 Natoma St, San Francisco.
articles.summary: Changelog在PlanetScale旧金山总部举办线下活动，聚焦AI、开发工具与开发者实践。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com联合创始人提出多数开源仓库或已被攻陷，并讨论AI冲击下开源与闭源的抉择。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale CEO谈5美元Postgres、智能体提交schema变更及500TB表秒级回滚。

articles.title: Several Waymo Self-Driving Cars Stalled in Traffic as San Francisco's Streets Flooded
articles.content: San Francisco's streets flooded this week after heavy rainfall — confusing several Waymo self-driving cars. The San Francisco blog Sfist describes what happened after the flooding in some places rose as high as three feet: Two lanes of Oak Street by the Golden Gate Park Panhandle were flooded Wednesday morning, with water spouting out of manhole covers, leading to a traffic backup that was made worse by a Waymo that couldn't figure its way out of the situation. The Waymo vehicle came to a stop in front of the spouting water, blocking one of the only passable lanes and worsening the traffic situation, as seen in the video below that is going viral... ["Other drivers had to veer into deeper water to weave around it," reports the San Francisco Chronicle.] Elsewhere in the city, Waymo rider Edward Frazer posted the video below to X, also around 10:20 am, saying that he had been in a Waymo for an hour and a half trying to get from North Beach to Mission Bay, with the vehicle pulling over around 10 times as it encountered flooded streets. The video shows the Waymo on what appears to be Townsend Street near Adobe's headquarters, stalled as water puddles in front of it. Waymo subsequently suspended all service for the rest of the day. But "frozen robotaxis were already clogging San Francisco streets by the time Waymo decided to rein in the fleet," reports the San Francisco Chronicle: Rider Amy Gutierrez said her Waymo suddenly stopped on Fell Street at the intersection of Masonic Avenue, where rain was coursing into rivers. She contacted company support and was transferred to three specialists who tried to move the jammed vehicle. It took a half-hour of false starts before they managed to remotely maneuver it to the right lane. "We were kind of just stuck there — cars were honking," she said, and other drivers were frustrated as traffic backed up. "One person drove by smacking their window, like 'Get out of the way.'" Or, as the New York Post puts it, "Waymos spark terror a
articles.summary: 旧金山暴雨内涝，多辆Waymo自动驾驶车在积水中停滞，暴露极端天气下的应对短板。

articles.title: US DOJ Charges Suspected Russian Agent for Stalking Palantir Employees in California
articles.content: America's Justice Department is prosecuting a suspected foreign agent in "a state-sponsored operation" that targeted tech workers in Palo Alto, California. "We will not tolerate any efforts — by foreign governments or otherwise — to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian. The alleged Russian agent was arrested in October for "stalking and harassing employees of the software and AI firm Palantir, sources told ABC News, because of its assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia." The indictment says D'iu traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City last June and was connected with a person who helped him illegally cross the southern U.S. border. Once in the U.S., he was instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones and remote access software that his co-conspirators used to help him in his alleged targeting of the company's employees. At one point, prosecutors say D'iu was directed by his co-conspirators to visit a coffee shop where many of the company's employees would work and try to identify them and take pictures of their screens while they were working... In September, prosecutors say D'iu allegedly followed a female employee of the company in his vehicle for nearly 30 miles after she left the company's Palo Alto, California, office. Even as the employee attempted various maneuvers to evade him, D'iu aggressively sought to follow her until she ultimately phoned police and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department's Mission Station. The nonprofit news site Palo Alto Online notes the government's affidavit "identified at least two other instances in early September in which employees of the defense company reported being followed by a car matching the description of D'iu's silver Lexus SUV. The coffee shops and other locations where D'iu stationed his laptop — sometimes for hours at a time — are in close proximity to the Palantir office in downtown Palo Alto... FBI agents executed a se
articles.summary: 美司法部起诉一名疑似俄方特工，其跟踪骚扰Palantir员工，涉国家支持的间谍行动。

articles.title: 59 Years Later, 'The Prisoner' is Getting a Second Remake - from Amazon Studios
articles.content: The Prisoner is getting a remake, reports ScreenRant. "Amazon Studios is currently developing a new and modern twist on the short-lived series..." ITV only aired 17 episodes of the original Prisoner back in 1967 and 1968, but it did receive a nomination for Best Dramatic Presentation at the Hugo Awards. Reviews were overwhelmingly positive... The Prisoner, considered one of the greatest sci-fi fantasy TV shows of all time, currently holds a perfect score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 93% with audiences. You can watch all 17 original episodes on YouTube. And apparently the production team for the remake "is apparently full of fans of the initial series," writes Inverse, citing an article from The Hollywood Reporter, "and ITV, the British TV network, is on board as well, which lends a little credence to it." More details on the remake from ScreenRant: Susan Montford, Don Murphy, Philippe Maigret, and Lucienne Papon have signed on as executive producers, but a showrunner has not been selected yet... Murphy has produced every single live-action Transformers movie, as well as the animated flick Transformers One. He also worked with Montford on Real Steel, Shoot 'Em Up, While She Was Out, and Vampire Academy... There have been attempts in the past to create a movie based on The Prisoner, with big names like Christopher Nolan, Ridley Scott, and Simon West all interested at various points, but nothing ever materialized... It took 41 years after the end of The Prisoner for any remake to finally make it to air. The six-episode 2009 miniseries had a solid cast that included Ian McKellen... McKellen and cinematographer Florian Hoffmeister even scored Emmy nominations. Unfortunately, reviews weren't kind to the show, which has a very low 17% critic score and 41% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the news. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 亚马逊工作室将翻拍1967年经典剧集《囚徒》，为该IP第二次重启。

articles.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to Standardize Parts to Lower Costs
articles.content: Car and Driver reports: Japan's three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News... In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car... The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan's seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. Long-time Slashdot reader sinij asks a related question. "Can we get a standard infotainment port/spec so we can have third-party market for this? Just like we used to have for stereo systems?" Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 丰田、日产、本田同意统一零部件标准，先从钢材与塑料规范入手以降低成本。

articles.title: Americans Enters Post-Penny World, Businesses Now Allowed to Round Cash Transactions to Nearest Nickel
articles.content: Friday U.S. President Trump "signed the Common Cents Act, which now lets businesses round cash transactions to the nearest nickel, into law," reports CBS News: It sets standards for cash transactions that businesses and consumers can use when exact change isn't available, as the penny is phased out. The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents... Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor. CBS includes this quote from an official NACS, an advocacy group for the convenience/fuel retailing industry. "Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended. NBC News points out that the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector's versions of pennies in "limited quantities," reporting on what has and hasn't changed now: The penny can still be used as legal tender "for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues," according to the new law. The Treasury Department said last year that the Federal Reserve will continue to recirculate the approximately 114 billion pennies that are in existence "for as long as possible...." And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint's currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel [according to the newly-signed law]. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 特朗普签署法案，美国进入后便士时代，商家可将现金交易四舍五入至最接近的5美分。

articles.title: Will AI-Fueled Cyberattacks Lead to Better Funding for Critical Open Source Projects?
articles.content: Remember that famous XKCD comic joking that all modern digital infrastructure rests on "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." Politico Europe's cybersecurity reporter wonders if this recent spate of outages suggests that supporting block is coming loose? (Especially after Politico reported Thursday that internal services at EU institutions went offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack.) This small army of largely volunteer coders now say they can't keep up with the power and pace of AI. articles.title: Earth has a New Moon
articles.content: "Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN: Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." The catalog of these visitors is relatively short because they usually slip under the radar... The exact origin of the space rock is "an active area of inquiry," Payne said, but most NEOs originate from the asteroid belt, a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter that contains millions of rocky objects of varying size that revolve around the sun. Over millions of years, gravitational forces can shift some of these objects' orbits toward the inner solar system. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit "digital library" that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board. The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED. "We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Sometimes three boring statements beats one clever expression
articles.content: Modern JavaScript gives us a lot of expressive tools. Sometimes a little too many. Optional chaining, nullish coalescing, ternaries, spread, template literals. I like all of them and use them every day. But together, they make it really easy to cram a lot of logic into a single expression. I used to think that was a sign of good JavaScript. I’m not so sure anymore. When one more ?? is too many Take something like this: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? defaults.theme; I’ve written this plenty of times. It’s short and it works. But once these expressions start growing, they read more like puzzles than code: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? getFallbackTheme() ?? defaults.theme; I can follow it, but I have to stop and parse it. Compare that to this: let theme = config?.theme; if (theme == null) { theme = user?.preferences?.theme; } if (theme == null) { theme = getFallbackTheme(); } return theme ?? defaults.theme; More lines? Sure. But it’s a lot more obvious. Yes, I give up const and reassign a variable. I’ll take that trade. Long expressions hide decisions Longer expressions squeeze several decisions into one piece of syntax. The more you chain, the more you have to work out at once: What happens if config is undefined? Where does the fallback come from? Which value wins? What if getFallbackTheme() throws? Chaining saves some vertical space, but you have to hold more in your head. It’s a practical problem, too. You can’t put a breakpoint on one fallback in the middle of a ?? chain, and you can’t log a single step without rewriting the expression. With separate statements, every step gets its own line to stop on or log. The diffs are nicer, as well. Adding a fallback means adding a block, not editing one dense line. Plain statements are fine A lot of us started treating plain if statements as something to avoid. So we’d rather write this: return user?.isAdmin ? getDashboard(user) : getLandingPage(user); than this: if (user?.isAdmin) { return getDashboard(user); } return getLandingPage(user); Neither one is objectively better. The second isn’t “less modern,” it’s often just easier to read. A single ternary like that is fine. It’s when they nest that I stop: return isLoading ? "Loading" : error ? "Failed to load" : items.length === 0 ? "Nothing here yet" : `${items.length} items`; The same thing with plain statements: if (isLoading) return "Loading"; if (error) return "Failed to load"; if (items.length === 0) return "Nothing here yet"; return `${items.length} items`; Clever code gets old fast Over the past couple of years I’ve found myself chaining less and writing fewer nested ternaries. I don’t mind adding another if anymore. I care more about readability than being clever. When I’m debugging production code or reviewing a pull request, I can’t remember ever wishing something had been written as one bigger expression. My rule of thumb is simple.
